interfaces.name: Two-sample mean testing problem
interfaces.type_shape: Two sample populations with different possible means and the same finite positive-definite covariance. Do not substitute the unequal-covariance extension mentioned as future work.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Two sample populations with different possible means and the same finite positive-definite covariance. Do not substitute the unequal-covariance extension mentioned as future work.

members.statement_original:
Suppose that for $m=1,2$, $\mathbf x_{mi}$, $i=1,\ldots,n_m$ is a random sample from a $p$-dimensional population with mean $\boldsymbol\mu_m$ and covariance matrix $\mathbf\Sigma$, which is assumed to be finite and positive definite.

Consider the two-sample mean testing problem:
\[
H_0:\boldsymbol\mu_1=\boldsymbol\mu_2\quad\text{versus}\quad H_1:\boldsymbol\mu_1\ne\boldsymbol\mu_2.
\]

interfaces.name: Pooled sample covariance matrix
interfaces.type_shape: Pooled covariance with denominator n1+n2−2 and separately centered groups. Sample means and covariance use the same observations as the statistic.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Pooled covariance with denominator n1+n2−2 and separately centered groups. Sample means and covariance use the same observations as the statistic.

members.statement_original:
Let $\bar{\mathbf x}_m=n_m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_m}\mathbf x_{mi}$ be the sample mean of the $m$th sample, and
\[
\mathbf S=(s_{hk})_{h,k=1,\ldots,p}=(n_1+n_2-2)^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^2\sum_{i=1}^{n_m}(\mathbf x_{mi}-\bar{\mathbf x}_m)(\mathbf x_{mi}-\bar{\mathbf x}_m)^T,
\]
be the pooled sample covariance matrix and $\mathbf x_{mi}=(x_{mi1},\ldots,x_{mip})^T$.

interfaces.name: Correlation matrix
interfaces.type_shape: Population correlation versus precision decomposition. D is the marginal variance diagonal, unrelated to D0 and D1 in Theorem 2.2.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Population correlation versus precision decomposition. D is the marginal variance diagonal, unrelated to D0 and D1 in Theorem 2.2.

members.statement_original: Decompose the covariance matrix $\mathbf\Sigma=\mathbf D^{1/2}\mathbf R\mathbf D^{1/2}$, where $\mathbf D$ is the diagonal matrix from the diagonal elements of $\mathbf\Sigma$, and $\mathbf R$ is the correlation matrix. The natural estimator of $\mathbf D$ is $\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf S)$, which is the diagonal matrix consisting of the diagonal elements of the pooled sample covariance matrix $\mathbf S$. Therefore, we focus on modeling $\mathbf R^{-1}$ instead of $\mathbf\Sigma^{-1}$.

interfaces.name: Symmetric matrix bases
interfaces.type_shape: Exact finite linear structure in known symmetric matrix bases. The true active set is assumed included; K is finite as clarified in the Discussion. No positive-definiteness constraint on fitted coefficients is supplied here.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Exact finite linear structure in known symmetric matrix bases. The true active set is assumed included; K is finite as clarified in the Discussion. No positive-definiteness constraint on fitted coefficients is supplied here.

members.statement_original: Let $\widehat{\mathbf R}$ denote the sample correlation matrix, that is, $\widehat{\mathbf R}=[\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf S)]^{-1/2}\mathbf S[\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf S)]^{-1/2}$.

interfaces.name: Quadratic loss
interfaces.type_shape: Unpenalized coefficient estimator. Preserve trace of the matrix residual squared; do not replace it by a Frobenius norm of a nonsymmetric residual. This B is sample-based, distinct from the B redefined in Theorem 2.2. Invertibility and coefficient identifiability are implicit.

members.statement_original:
Next, we propose an estimation procedure for $\boldsymbol\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_K)^T$.

To estimate $\boldsymbol\theta$, we aim to minimize the quadratic loss given by
\[
\min_{\boldsymbol\theta}\operatorname{tr}[\widehat{\mathbf R}(\theta_1\mathbf A_1+\cdots+\theta_K\mathbf A_K)-\mathbf I_p]^2.
\]
(4)
Here, $\operatorname{tr}(\cdot)$ refers to the trace of a matrix. Denote $\mathbf B$ to be a $K\times K$ matrix, with $(k,l)$-element given by $p^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(\widehat{\mathbf R}\mathbf A_k\widehat{\mathbf R}\mathbf A_l)$, and $\mathbf b$ to be a $K\times1$ vector, with the $k$th element being $p^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(\widehat{\mathbf R}\mathbf A_k)$. The minimizer of (4) is $\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}=\mathbf B^{-1}\mathbf b$.

interfaces.semantic_boundary: Finite aspect-ratio limit, with n=n1+n2 and p,n tending to infinity in the proof context. The printed statement allows y=1 although Theorem 2.2 contains (1−y)^{-2}; no exclusion is added.

members.statement_original: Denote $y_{n-2}=p/(n-2)$, and assume $y=\lim_{n\to\infty}y_{n-2}$ exists and is finite.

naming_context.text: Bai and Saranadasa (1996) studied the asymptotical behavior of the Hotelling $T^2$ test and concluded that it has no power when $p/n$ approaches to 1 due to effect of high dimension.

members.statement_original: Although Theorems 2.3–2.4 in this paper require the bounded spectral norm of the population correlation matrix, the restrictions may be relaxed following the proof of Theorems 2.2–2.3 in Zheng et al. (2019), which removes the bounded spectral norm restriction. Because the proof of the central limit theorem under the bounded spectral norm is very different from the proof of the central limit theorem under the unbounded spectral norm, we place the proof under the unbounded spectral norm in future work.
